Attention: Megan Wells, Director of Operations
Dear Ms. Wells:

We are glad that Sullivan, Hall and Kelly has asked us to look closely at its revenue cycle, and we are writing to set down, in one place and in plain language, the understanding on which we will carry out that work, so that what we believe we have been engaged to do and the terms on which we have agreed to do it match, in every particular, what you understand them to be. Our purpose in writing is not to paper the relationship but to make certain that we begin it already agreed on its shape, and if any line below reads differently from the conversations we have had with you, we would be glad to hear about it and to revise it before you sign.
The Work You Have Asked Us to Do

You have asked us to diagnose your revenue cycle from end to end and to tell you, with figures you can stand behind, where it is losing money that it ought to be keeping. We will follow a claim from the moment a patient is registered through coding and charge capture, submission, payer adjudication, denial and appeal, and the collection of what remains, and at each of those points we will measure what is leaking, why it is leaking, and how much of it is genuinely recoverable, so that the conclusions we hand you rest on the cycle as your own data describes it rather than on our impressions of it.

So that the edges of the work sit on the page and not in anyone's memory, this is a diagnostic and not an implementation: we will tell you what we find and what we recommend, but installing new processes, renegotiating payer contracts, or standing up a denials-management function are each separate undertakings that would be the subject of their own letter. The study reaches only the revenue cycle of the operations you have named for us, it does not opine on the fair market value of any physician arrangement, and it is neither an audit of your financial statements nor an assurance of any kind upon them.
How We Mean to Go About It

We expect the work to move through three unhurried phases, and we describe them here so that you know what to expect of us and, roughly, in what order they will come. In the first we will gather and reconcile the source data alongside your billing and operations staff and agree with them, in writing, on the definitions we are working from, because a revenue-cycle study is only ever as sound as the boundaries drawn around each measure it reports.

In the second we will work through the leakage point by point, testing each apparent loss before we rely on it and separating the losses that are genuinely recoverable from those that are simply the cost of doing business with a given payer. In the third we will write our report, review a draft of it with you so that any factual error about your operations is caught and corrected before the document is final, and deliver our findings with the recommendations that follow them kept plainly distinct and labeled as recommendations.
Who Will Be Doing the Work

Susan Clark, a Principal in our advisory practice, will lead the engagement and be your point of contact on any question of finding or method; she is careful with the language of a report to a degree your general counsel will appreciate, and she will put her name to what we deliver. Daniel Alvarado, also a Principal, will carry the economics of the cycle, reconciling the cost and payer detail until each line of it tells the truth, and you and your team will see a good deal of both of them as the work proceeds.

I will keep a partner's eye on the engagement from beginning to end and will remain available to you on any matter of scope, staffing, or terms. If at any point the work or the people are not serving you as they should, I would ask that you bring it to me early, and a quiet word is very often all it takes for us to put a small thing right.
Fee and Commencement

Our fee for the work described above is {{fact:f:E-2024-001.fee}}, fixed for that scope, and we are prepared to begin on {{fact:f:E-2024-001.start}}. Should you ask anything of us that falls outside the scope set out here, we will tell you so in writing and quote it to you separately, and we will take it up only once you have asked us, in writing, to proceed.
Fees and Payment

We will bill against the fixed fee monthly as the work goes forward, and each invoice falls due within thirty days of its date. Any out-of-pocket costs are billed at cost and sit outside the fixed fee, and should a question ever arise about an invoice we would ask you to bring it to us directly and plainly, as we will bring any question of ours to you.
Term and Termination

The engagement begins on the date named above and continues until we have delivered our final report and you have settled the fee for it. Either of us may end it on written notice, in which case you would owe us for the work properly done and the costs incurred to the point of notice, and we may also step back where our professional obligations require it, including were we ever asked to state a conclusion the analysis does not support, which is not a report this firm will sign.
Confidentiality

We will treat what you share with us as confidential, use it only for this study, and hold our findings and our report in the same confidence, keeping your data within the small team named above and disposing of it properly once the work is done. Because revenue-cycle data carries patient and financial detail of a kind that must travel carefully, we would ask that any question of wider distribution of our report come through us first, so that we can point out anything that ought not to circulate freely.
Limitation of Liability

Our total liability arising out of this engagement is limited to the fees actually paid to us under it, and we are not responsible for indirect or consequential losses, lost revenue among them. We say this plainly rather than in fine print, because a diagnostic is a considered judgment formed on the data available at a moment in time, and it cannot promise a recovery that depends on decisions, payers, and conditions lying outside our work; what you engage from us is our care and our judgment, honestly exercised and set out with their limits, and that is exactly what we undertake to give you.
Governing Law

This letter and the work it describes are governed by the law of the state in which our firm keeps its principal office, without regard to its conflict-of-laws rules. Were a disagreement over fees ever to arise between us, we would each take part in that state bar's fee-dispute process before either of us carried the matter any further.

If this letter sets out our understanding correctly, we would be grateful if you would sign the enclosed copy and return it to us, keeping the second for your own records; on receiving it, Susan Clark will be in touch to arrange the opening session and our first request for data. We are glad to be taking up this work for Sullivan, Hall and Kelly, and we look forward to being of genuine and lasting use to you.
To: Daniel Alvarado, Principal
From: Susan Clark, Principal
Re: Kickoff, Revenue Cycle Diagnostic for Sullivan, Hall and Kelly

Our charge on this engagement is narrow and worth stating at the outset: we are to tell {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} where its revenue cycle is losing money it should be keeping, and to do it with figures that reconcile to its own general ledger rather than sit beside it. The work begins on {{fact:f:E-2024-001.start}}, and I want us aligned on how it will run before then, because the diagnostic itself is not difficult so much as it is exacting, and most of that exactness lives in getting the definitions and the data right before we build anything on them.

A word on register, since we will spend real time in front of their billing and operations people and, in the end, their counsel: we write for that audience throughout, which means we lead with the finding and let the recommendation follow it, labeled as a recommendation, and we do not call a loss recoverable until we have shown on the data that it is.

The distinction that will carry the most weight in the report is between money we can demonstrate is recoverable and money that is only the price of a given payer relationship, and we will draw that line conservatively, so that every dollar we place on the recoverable side of it can be defended to someone who is looking for the reason it should not be there.

On the data itself, Sullivan, Hall and Kelly runs a modern billing system and their extracts should reach us clean, so I do not expect us to lose days chasing files. The exception is the health system's contracting office, which prints, signs, and scans, so a handful of executed statements and consents will come to us as images with no text behind them, and those we will read and key by hand rather than pull.
I have set the lines of work out below, with an owner against each. None of it is heavy in the first weeks, so this is the moment to tell me if any of it looks wrong to you.
How the Diagnostic Breaks Down

items: Data assembly and reconciliation. Owner: Susan Clark. Pull the claim-level detail, remittances, and adjustment and write-off data from their billing system, by payer and service line, and reconcile it to the general ledger before we measure anything against it.
Front-end losses. Owner: Susan Clark. Measure the revenue lost at registration and eligibility, meaning unverified coverage, missing authorizations, and the denials that trace directly back to them.
Coding and charge capture. Owner: Daniel Alvarado. Test whether the charges billed match the care documented, and size undercoding and missed charges separately from outright denials.

Denials and appeals. Owner: Daniel Alvarado. Categorize denials by cause and payer, measure the share worked against the share written off unappealed, and estimate what a disciplined appeals process would recover.

Aged receivables and payer underpayment. Owner: Susan Clark. Age the receivables, isolate the payers running slow, and check paid claims against contracted rates to find the underpayment the cycle is not catching.

blocks.text: First Moves

items: I will send Sullivan, Hall and Kelly our data request this week, so their billing team has time to assemble the extracts before we start.
Daniel Alvarado to confirm the denial taxonomy we will code to, so we categorize the population once and not twice.
We will hold a short standing check-in each week, so that small questions do not wait a fortnight to surface.
Megan Wells, their Director of Operations, is our client contact; please route anything client-facing through me, so that she hears one voice from us.

blocks.text: That is the plan as it stands. The value in these first weeks is in the definitions and the reconciliation and not in the arithmetic, and I will keep this memo current if any of it shifts.
Minutes of our working session on the revenue cycle diagnostic for Sullivan, Hall and Kelly. Recorded by Daniel Alvarado.
Attendees

items: Daniel Alvarado, Principal, Advisory
Susan Clark, Principal, Advisory
Megan Wells, Director of Operations, Sullivan, Hall and Kelly

blocks.text: Discussion

We have a base we can trust, which was the thing we most needed before drawing any conclusion. The claim and remittance data now reconciles to the ledger {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} keeps. From here the work is measurement, not assembly.

The scanned documents cost us a little time, as we expected they would. The contracting office's executed statements reached us as images with no text, so Susan Clark had them read and keyed by hand. It was a small delay and it is behind us now.

The denial pattern is the first thing worth naming, though we are naming it as a finding to confirm and not a conclusion. A large share of denials trace to the front end, to eligibility and authorization, rather than to coding. If that holds, the fix sits earlier in the cycle than the client had expected.

The receivables tell a related story. One commercial payer is running well past its peers on days in AR, and the aging is concentrated there rather than spread across the book. We want to separate slow from denied before we say anything more about it.

The write-off data is worth a careful look, and we have started on it. A share of what has been written off was never appealed, and some of that may have been recoverable. We are not ready to put a number on it yet, only to say the category is real.

Charge capture looks cleaner than the denials on first read. The charges we sampled match the documentation, so undercoding may be the smaller problem here. We will still size it before we set it aside.

Megan Wells walked us through how registration actually runs on the floor, which changed how we read the eligibility denials. Some of what looks like a process gap is a system that does not carry an authorization field where the staff would use it. That is a useful distinction, and it points at a different remedy.

We also agreed to hold the scope where it is. There is a temptation to drift into fixing the front end while we are in it, and we are resisting it. The diagnostic tells the client where the losses sit; the remedy is a separate conversation, and we said as much to Megan Wells.

We are keeping recommendations out of these minutes on purpose. They belong in the report, set after the findings that carry them. For now the two open items are the denial causes and the underpayment check, and we hold the next session once both are tested. Nothing agreed here is left to memory; the items below carry an owner against each.
Action Items

rows: Confirm the share of denials originating in eligibility and authorization
Separate slow-paying receivables from denied ones for the outlier payer
Key the remaining scanned statements from the contracting office
Check paid claims against contracted rates for the top three payers
Send Sullivan, Hall and Kelly our questions on the registration workflow

blocks.text: Status Report: Revenue Cycle Diagnostic for Sullivan, Hall and Kelly
Prepared for {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} by Susan Clark, Principal, and reviewed by Daniel Alvarado, Principal, before it was sent.
Where the Work Stands

The diagnostic is at its midpoint and on plan. The claim, remittance, and adjustment data now reconciles to your general ledger, which gives us a measured base rather than an impression, and the work from here is confirmation of what that base is telling us rather than any further assembly. Nothing in this report is a final finding, and we have marked plainly what is settled and what we are still testing.

The extracts your billing team provided came to us clean, which has kept us on schedule, and the only real handwork has been on the executed statements and consents that your contracting office prints and scans, which reach us as images and which we have read and keyed by hand rather than pulled. That work is complete, and it was never on the critical path.

One point of method is worth stating early, because it governs how you should read every figure that follows. We are drawing a firm line between the money we can demonstrate is recoverable and the money that is simply the price of a given payer relationship, and we are counting only the first of those as a loss you can act on, so the recoverable figures in this and the final report are the conservative ones and are meant to be defensible line by line.
Completed This Period
The work this period was assembly and first analysis, and we completed the following.

items: Assembled and reconciled the claim-level detail, remittances, and write-off data to your general ledger, by payer and service line, so that every figure we report can be traced back to a source.
Categorized the denial population by cause and payer, and established a first read that a large share of denials originate at the front end, in eligibility and authorization, rather than in coding.
Aged the receivables and isolated a single commercial payer running well past its peers, and began separating genuinely slow payment from denied claims caught in the same aging.
Sampled charge capture against clinical documentation and found it broadly sound, which lets us weigh undercoding as the smaller of the losses rather than the larger.

blocks.text: The Period Ahead
The next period turns from measuring the cycle to confirming what those measures mean, and we plan to do the following.

items: Confirm the share of denials that begin in eligibility and authorization, and quantify the revenue that a disciplined front-end check would protect.
Complete the underpayment check, comparing paid claims against contracted rates for your largest payers, since a payer paying below contract is a loss the cycle does not currently flag.
Size the recoverable portion of the aged receivables for the outlier payer, kept separate from what is merely slow to pay.
Draft the findings, with each recommendation set apart and labeled as a recommendation, and review a draft with your team before anything is called final.

blocks.text: What We Need From You
Two things from your team would keep us on the current pace, and neither is urgent this week, so we set them out now while there is time to gather them.

items: The eligibility and authorization detail behind the denied claims, so that we can confirm how much of the front-end loss your system is already recording and how much of it goes uncaptured.

A short session with whoever owns your payer contracts, so that the rates we test paid claims against are the rates you are actually owed rather than the ones we have had to infer from the remittances.

blocks.text: Risks and Watch Items
Three items could still move the findings, and we want them on your radar.

items: Front-end data. Our read that denials begin at registration depends on the eligibility and authorization detail your system records, and where that detail is not captured we will say so and treat the estimate as a floor.
Contracted rates. The underpayment check is only as good as the rate schedules we are given, and any schedule we cannot obtain is a gap we will flag rather than fill with an assumption.
Completeness. Our conclusions describe the cycle as your data describes it to us, so a material gap in the source data is a limit on the finding, which we will state plainly rather than paper over.

blocks.text: Budget

The engagement is running against its fixed budget of {{fact:f:E-2024-001.fee}}, and the effort spent to date is roughly half of it, which is where it should sit at the halfway mark. No part of the work so far has fallen outside the scope set in our engagement letter, and we would tell you in writing before taking up anything that did.

Our next report will carry the tested findings on the front-end denials and the underpayment check, which are the two questions that will most shape the recommendations. If anything in your operations changed during this period that we should factor in, we would ask you to tell us before we begin to draft.
Minutes of our working session on the revenue cycle diagnostic for Sullivan, Hall and Kelly. Recorded by Daniel Alvarado.

Susan Clark, Principal, Advisory

blocks.text: Discussion

The findings hold, and we are into drafting rather than analysis. The reconciliation ties at every line to the ledger {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} keeps, and nothing in the final data moved a conclusion. This was the session where we agreed what the report will say.

The front end is where the money is, and we can say so now with the data behind us. The larger share of recoverable denials begins at eligibility and authorization, not at coding, and a disciplined front-end check would protect most of it. That is the headline finding.

The underpayment check turned up a second, quieter loss. One payer is paying below its contracted rate on a specific class of claim, and the cycle has not been catching it. Susan Clark has that quantified and tied back to the contract.

The receivables came out where we thought they would. The outlier payer was slow more than it was denying, and the genuinely recoverable piece is smaller than the aging first suggested. We have it separated now, slow from denied, and only the denied share sits in the recoverable figure.

We were careful, as we always are, to separate what is recoverable from what is not. Some of the write-offs we examined are simply the price of certain payer relationships, and we will not dress those up as recoverable. The recoverable figure in the report is the conservative one, and we can defend every dollar of it.
The scanned statements are all keyed now, and nothing in them changed a finding. They mattered for completeness more than for the numbers. It was worth doing by hand, and it is done.

Megan Wells asked whether the front-end finding means the client should reorganize registration. We were careful with the line between finding and recommendation. Our finding is that recoverable denials begin at the front end, and what the client does about that is the client's decision; the report will label our recommendation as a recommendation, kept apart from the finding it rests on.

We agreed the shape of the report. Findings first, recommendations after and labeled as such, and the underpayment detail documented in an appendix so the client can see the working. Susan Clark and I will square away the tables while the drafting is under way, and we will bring a draft to Sullivan, Hall and Kelly for a factual read before anything is called final.
On pace, we are in the last stretch, and what remains is drafting and review rather than analysis. Nothing agreed here is left to memory; the items below carry an owner against each.
Action Items

rows: Draft the findings section, with recommendations set apart and labeled
Finalize the recoverable-denials figure and the assumption log
Document the payer underpayment detail for the appendix
Lay out the front-end options without ranking them
Schedule the draft review with the client
